name: People of Nuh
story: Nuh called his people to worship Allah alone for 950 years (29:14). Their leaders mocked the poor who followed him and clung to their idols Wadd, Suwa, Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr (71:23). Only a few believed, and Allah told Nuh to build the ark.
end: The Flood drowned the disbelievers, Nuh's own son among them, and the ark came to rest on al-Judi (11:42-44).
lesson: Numbers and status do not make people right: the few who believed were saved and the many were lost.
archaeology: Excavations at Ur, Kish and Shuruppak found flood layers, but from different dates, so they show local floods rather than one event. Mesopotamian poems such as Atrahasis and Gilgamesh also tell of a great flood.
note: The Quran does not name Nuh's land; Iraq is the commentators' view. Al-Judi is often identified with Mount Cudi in south-east Turkey.

name: Ad
story: Ad were a mighty people of the sand dunes who built tall monuments and boasted, 'Who is greater than us in strength?' (41:15). Hud, one of their own, called them to worship Allah and give up their tyranny. They mocked him and said some of their gods had struck him with evil (11:54).
end: Allah sent a screaming, violent wind for seven nights and eight days that left them like hollow trunks of palm trees (69:6-7).
lesson: Strength and great buildings cannot protect a people who are arrogant towards their Creator.
archaeology: In 1992 a team guided by satellite images found a caravan fort at Shisr in Oman and announced it as Ubar, often linked with Iram. Many scholars doubt the link, and Ad remain unidentified by archaeology.
note: Scholars differ whether Iram (89:7) was a city, a tribe or an ancestor of Ad.

name: Thamud
story: Thamud came after Ad and carved their homes from the mountains (15:82). Their brother Salih called them to Allah, and they demanded a sign. A she-camel was given to them, with her own day to drink. The worst of them hamstrung her and dared Salih to bring the punishment (7:77).
end: After three days a mighty blast and an earthquake seized them, and they lay dead in their homes (11:65-67).
lesson: Signs are a test, and rejecting a clear sign brings ruin.
archaeology: Assyrian records of Sargon II (c. 715 BCE) and later Greek and Roman writers mention Thamud. The grand tombs seen at Hegra (Mada'in Salih) today are Nabataean, cut around the 1st century, so they are later than the Thamud of the Quran.
note: The Prophet ﷺ passed al-Hijr on the way to Tabuk and told his Companions not to enter the homes of the punished except weeping (Reported by Bukhari).

name: People of Lut
story: Lut, the nephew of Ibrahim, lived among a people who openly practised a shameless act no nation had done before (7:80) and robbed travellers on the road (29:29). When angels came to Lut as guests, the men rushed to seize them. Only Lut's family left by night, and his wife stayed behind.
end: Allah turned their towns upside down and rained on them stones of layered hard clay (11:82).
lesson: A society that makes open shamelessness its custom invites the fate of those before it.
archaeology: Sodom is usually sought near the Dead Sea; candidates include Bab edh-Dhra and Tall el-Hammam in Jordan. A 2021 study proposed that an airburst destroyed Tall el-Hammam around 1650 BCE, but the claim is strongly disputed.
note: The name Sodom comes from the Bible; the Quran calls the towns 'the overturned' (9:70, 53:53) and says their ruins lie on a road still travelled (15:76).

name: Madyan
story: Madyan were traders on the caravan routes who cheated in weights and measures and blocked people from Allah's path. Their brother Shuayb told them to give full measure. They asked whether his prayer told him that they must leave their fathers' gods and stop doing as they pleased with their wealth (11:87). Later, Musa found refuge in Madyan and married there.
end: An earthquake and a mighty blast seized them, and they lay dead in their homes as if they had never lived there (7:91-92, 11:94-95).
lesson: Honesty in trade is part of faith, not a separate matter.
archaeology: Ptolemy's geography places a town called Modiana near the Gulf of Aqaba. At al-Bad' in Saudi Arabia, rock-cut tombs known as Maghayir Shuayb, 'the caves of Shuayb', are Nabataean in style; the Bible's Midianites lived in this region.

name: Companions of the Thicket
story: A people of a wooded land to whom Shuayb was sent. Like Madyan, they cheated in measure and weight, and Shuayb told them to weigh with an even balance (26:181-182). They called him bewitched and dared him to bring down a piece of the sky on them (26:185-187).
end: The punishment of the day of the black cloud seized them (26:189).
lesson: Mocking a warning does not make the danger go away.
archaeology: No site has been identified. Aykah means a thicket of dense trees; some writers link it to the oases of the Tabuk region near the Gulf of Aqaba.
note: Scholars differ: some say they were Madyan under another name, others a separate people. In Surah al-Shuara Shuayb is not called their 'brother' (26:177), which some take as a sign they were different.

name: Companions of the Rass
story: The Quran names them twice among the nations that denied their messengers, beside the people of Nuh, Ad and Thamud (25:38, 50:12). It gives no details of their messenger or their sins.
end: Allah says He destroyed each of these nations completely (25:39).
lesson: Even nations whose stories are forgotten were warned before they were judged.
archaeology: No site is known. Rass means a well or pit; commentators suggested places in Najd and Yamamah, or the region of the Aras river, but none is confirmed.
note: Their identity is unknown, and the stories told about them in the commentaries are weak or contradictory.

name: People of Tubba
story: Tubba was the title of the kings of Himyar in Yemen. The Quran asks the Makkans whether they are better than the people of Tubba, a strong nation destroyed for their crimes (44:37). Commentators say one Tubba visited Yathrib and Makkah and honoured the Kaaba.
end: They were destroyed for their crimes, though the Quran does not say how (44:37).
lesson: Power that once seemed permanent can vanish, as Himyar's did.
archaeology: Hundreds of Himyarite inscriptions from Zafar and across Yemen record kings who ruled from about 110 BCE to 525 CE. From around 380 CE they left the old gods for one God, whom they called Rahmanan.
note: Which Tubba is meant comes from the commentators. A narration says not to curse Tubba because he had become Muslim; scholars differ on its strength.

name: Saba (Sheba)
story: The hoopoe told Sulayman of a queen of Saba who worshipped the sun with her people (27:22-24). She came to Sulayman and submitted with him to Allah. Later generations lived between two gardens around Ma'rib, in a good land with a forgiving Lord, but turned away from gratitude.
end: Allah sent the flood of the dam upon them; their gardens became bitter scrub and their people were scattered across the land (34:16-19).
lesson: Blessings are kept by gratitude and lost by turning away.
archaeology: The great dam of Ma'rib, whose stone sluices still stand, watered the oasis for over a thousand years. Inscriptions record its repairs, including one by Abraha in 548, before it finally failed around the late 6th century.
note: The queen's name, Bilqis, comes from the commentators, not the Quran.

name: Bani Israil
story: The children of Yaqub, who was also called Israil. Allah saved them from Firaun, gave them the Torah and sent them prophet after prophet, from Musa to Isa. The Quran recalls both their favours and their failures: the calf, refusing to enter the Holy Land, and breaking their covenants.
end: They were not destroyed as one nation. The Quran says they would spread corruption twice and be punished each time (17:4-7), and that some of them remained upright (7:159).
lesson: Being chosen is a trust that must be kept, not a privilege of birth.
archaeology: The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) is the oldest known mention of 'Israel', and the Tel Dan inscription (9th century BCE) mentions the 'House of David'. There is no direct archaeological evidence of the Exodus, and its date is debated.

name: People of Firaun
story: Firaun ruled Egypt, enslaved Bani Israil and killed their sons (28:4). Musa and Harun brought him clear signs, and his own magicians believed. His court and people followed him in arrogance, even as floods, locusts, lice, frogs and blood struck them (7:133).
end: Firaun and his army drowned in the sea while chasing Bani Israil, and his body was preserved as a sign for those after him (10:90-92).
lesson: Following a tyrant does not excuse those who choose to follow him.
archaeology: Which Pharaoh opposed Musa is unknown. Ramesses II and his son Merneptah are common guesses, but Egyptian records do not mention the Exodus.
note: In Yusuf's story the ruler is called 'the king' (12:43) and in Musa's story 'Firaun'; some note that 'pharaoh' became a title of the king only in the New Kingdom.

name: People of Yunus
story: Yunus was sent to a city of a hundred thousand or more (37:147). When they would not listen, he left them in anger before Allah allowed him, and was swallowed by the whale. After Allah saved him he returned, and found that his people had believed.
end: They are the only town in the Quran that believed when punishment drew near, and Allah lifted it from them (10:98).
lesson: Repentance can still change a people's fate while the door is open.
archaeology: The ruins of Nineveh lie at Mosul in Iraq. The shrine of Nabi Yunus stood on one of its mounds until it was blown up in 2014, and tunnels dug afterwards revealed an Assyrian palace beneath it.
note: The Quran does not name Nineveh; the identification comes from tradition and the Bible. In the seerah, the Prophet ﷺ called Yunus his brother when he met Addas, a man of Nineveh, at Ta'if.

name: The city of the Sleepers
story: A few young believers fled their city's idol worship and took refuge in a cave (18:14-16). Allah made them sleep for 309 years (18:25). When one went to buy food with old coins, the townspeople found them, and argued over building a place of worship over the cave (18:21).
end: The Quran tells of no punishment. Commentators say the city had become believing by the time they woke, and their waking became a proof of the Resurrection (18:21).
lesson: Allah protects those who hold to their faith, even when they must withdraw to keep it.
archaeology: Christian tradition places the Seven Sleepers at Ephesus in Turkey, fleeing the emperor Decius around 250 CE. A cave at al-Rajib near Amman, Jordan, with Byzantine tombs, was excavated in 1963 and is also proposed.
note: The Quran leaves their number open (18:22); their names and the identity of the city come from the commentators.

name: Companions of the Ditch
story: Believers who refused to give up their faith were thrown into a ditch of blazing fire while their persecutors sat watching (85:5-7). Their only crime was believing in Allah, the Mighty, the Praiseworthy (85:8). Historians link the story to Najran around 523, under the Himyarite king Dhu Nuwas.
end: The Quran curses the persecutors and promises them the punishment of Hell and of burning (85:4, 85:10).
lesson: Faith can be worth more than life itself.
archaeology: The ruins of al-Ukhdud at Najran preserve an ancient walled town. Syriac letters, the Book of the Himyarites and inscriptions of King Yusuf As'ar Yath'ar (Dhu Nuwas) record the killing of Najran's Christians around 523.
note: Some commentators connect the verses instead to the hadith of the boy and the king (Reported by Muslim), or to other events; scholars differ.

name: Companions of the Elephant
story: Abraha, the Aksumite ruler of Yemen, built a great church in San'a and marched on Makkah with an elephant to destroy the Kaaba. Abd al-Muttalib told him the House had a Lord who would protect it. The elephant knelt and would not move towards Makkah.
end: Allah sent flocks of birds that pelted the army with stones of hard clay, leaving them like eaten straw (105:3-5).
lesson: Allah protects His House, and no army can overrule Him.
archaeology: Abraha is a historical figure: his inscriptions at Ma'rib (548) and Murayghan (552) survive, the second recording a campaign into central Arabia. Whether that campaign was the Elephant, and whether the attack was in 570 or earlier, is debated.
note: The Year of the Elephant is the traditional year of the Prophet's ﷺ birth.

name: People of the Sabbath
story: A town of Bani Israil by the sea was forbidden to fish on the Sabbath. The fish came to them openly on the Sabbath and not on other days (7:163), so some found ways around the law. Some townspeople warned them, and others asked why they bothered to warn a people Allah would punish (7:164).
end: Those who defied the command were turned into despised apes, and those who forbade the evil were saved (7:165-166).
lesson: A trick to get around Allah's law is still disobedience.
archaeology: The Quran does not name the town; commentators often say Aylah, at today's Aqaba, where Roman and early Islamic towns have been excavated. Nothing found there relates to the story.
note: Commentators place it in the time of Dawud. Most say the change was real; Mujahid's view that it was a change of hearts is a minority opinion. The trick of setting nets on Friday comes from the commentators.

name: Yajuj and Majuj
story: Dhul-Qarnayn found a people between two mountains who complained that Yajuj and Majuj were spreading corruption in the land (18:94). He built a barrier of iron and molten copper that they could neither climb nor pierce (18:96-97), and said it would stand until his Lord's promise came.
end: Their end has not yet come. Near the Hour the barrier will give way and they will pour down from every height (21:96); the Prophet ﷺ said Allah will destroy them in the time of Isa (Reported by Muslim).
lesson: No wall stands forever; only Allah's promise is certain.
archaeology: Writers have linked the barrier to the Sasanian walls of Derbent in the Caucasus, the Caspian Gates, or the Iron Gate in Uzbekistan, but no barrier of iron and copper has been found.
note: Who they are is unknown. A hadith describes them as descendants of Adam (Reported by Bukhari).

name: Quraysh
story: The Prophet's ﷺ own tribe, keepers of the Kaaba and masters of the winter and summer caravans (106:2). Their leaders opposed him for twenty years, boycotted his clan, plotted to kill him (8:30) and fought him at Badr, Uhud and the Trench. Yet Khadijah and Abu Bakr, among the first believers, were also of Quraysh.
end: They were not destroyed. Makkah opened in 630 almost without fighting, the Prophet ﷺ forgave them, and Quraysh entered Islam; the first caliphs came from among them.
lesson: Even fierce enemies can become the carriers of the message.
archaeology: Little archaeology has been done in Makkah, and the Quraysh are known mainly from Arabic sources. A place called Macoraba in Ptolemy's geography is sometimes, but not certainly, identified with Makkah.
note: The start date is traditional: Qusayy ibn Kilab is said to have gathered Quraysh in Makkah in the 5th century.

name: Thaqif
story: The tribe of Ta'if, keepers of the shrine of the goddess al-Lat. In 619 the Prophet ﷺ went to them seeking support; their leaders refused and set boys to stone him until his feet bled. In 630 they fought him at Hunayn and then held out in a siege of Ta'if.
end: They were not destroyed. In 631 their delegation came to Madinah and accepted Islam, and the idol of al-Lat was pulled down.
lesson: The town that stoned the Prophet ﷺ became Muslim, because he prayed for its people instead of against them.
archaeology: Ta'if is a living mountain city where little excavation has been done. The goddess al-Lat is known from Nabataean and Palmyrene inscriptions across Arabia and Syria.
note: When the angel of the mountains offered to crush the people of the two mountains, the Prophet ﷺ refused, hoping their descendants would worship Allah (Reported by Bukhari and Muslim). Some commentators say the 'great man' of 43:31 was Urwah ibn Mas'ud of Thaqif.

name: Hawazin
story: A large confederation of tribes in the hills east of Makkah; the Prophet's ﷺ foster-mother Halimah came from one of its clans, the Banu Sa'd. After Makkah opened in 630, they gathered under Malik ibn Awf to attack the Muslims and ambushed them in the valley of Hunayn.
end: The Muslims, shaken at first, held firm around the Prophet ﷺ and won (9:25-26). Hawazin then accepted Islam, and the Prophet ﷺ returned their captives to them.
lesson: Victory comes from Allah, not from numbers, as the believers learned at Hunayn (9:25).
archaeology: Hawazin are known from Arabic sources and poetry, not from archaeology. Hunayn is traditionally placed in a valley on the road between Makkah and Ta'if.

name: Aws and Khazraj (the Ansar)
story: Two Arab tribes of Yathrib, long locked in feuds that ended in the battle of Bu'ath. Some of them met the Prophet ﷺ at Aqabah during the pilgrimage and pledged to protect him. When he emigrated in 622 they welcomed the emigrants and shared their homes and wealth with them.
end: They were not destroyed but honoured: Allah named them the Ansar, the Helpers, and joined their hearts after their enmity (3:103, 8:63).
lesson: Faith can turn old enemies into brothers.
archaeology: Yathrib appears in inscriptions of the Babylonian king Nabonidus, who lived at nearby Tayma in the 6th century BCE. The Quran calls the city Yathrib once (33:13).

name: The Romans (Rum)
story: Around 614 the Persians crushed the Byzantine Romans and took Jerusalem. The pagans of Makkah rejoiced, since the Romans were People of the Book. The Quran then foretold that the Romans would win within a few years, and that the believers would rejoice on that day (30:2-5).
end: The emperor Heraclius defeated Persia in 627-628, as foretold. The Byzantine Empire lasted until the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453.
lesson: Allah's promise comes true even when the odds look impossible.
archaeology: The Persian capture of Jerusalem (614) and Heraclius's victory near Nineveh (627) are well recorded by Byzantine, Syriac and Armenian chroniclers. 'The nearest land' (30:3) is usually read as Syria and Palestine; some modern writers read it as 'the lowest land', the Dead Sea basin.
note: Abu Bakr made a wager with Quraysh on this prophecy, before betting was forbidden (Reported by Tirmidhi).

name: The Persians
story: The Sasanian Persians were the other great power of the Prophet's ﷺ world. They defeated the Romans in his lifetime (30:2-3), and their emperor Khosrow tore up the letter the Prophet ﷺ sent him. When the verse about 'others of them who have not yet joined them' came (62:3), the Prophet ﷺ placed his hand on Salman the Persian.
end: Their empire fell to the Muslims after al-Qadisiyyah (636) and Nahavand (642), but the Persians themselves became pillars of Islam, giving it scholars such as Sibawayh, al-Ghazali and Fakhr al-Din al-Razi.
lesson: Empires fall, but a people who accept guidance can rise higher than their kings.
archaeology: The great arch of Taq Kasra at Ctesiphon, near Baghdad, still stands from the Sasanian palace. Rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam and Bishapur show Sasanian kings triumphing over Roman emperors.
note: The hadith 'if faith were at the Pleiades, men from these people would reach it' explains 62:3 (Reported by Bukhari and Muslim). The tearing of the letter is reported by Bukhari.

name: People of Ibrahim
story: Ibrahim's people, his father Azar among them, worshipped idols and the heavenly bodies. He argued with them, broke their idols and left the largest one standing (21:58). They threw him into a great fire, but Allah made it cool and safe for him (21:69).
end: The Quran describes no destruction of them. Ibrahim left them, saying he was emigrating to his Lord (29:26).
lesson: Truth can stand alone against a whole society.
archaeology: Ur was excavated by Leonard Woolley in 1922-34, revealing its ziggurat and royal tombs. The link between Ibrahim and Ur comes from the Bible ('Ur of the Chaldees'); Muslim tradition also names Kutha in Iraq and Urfa in Turkey.
note: The king who argued with Ibrahim (2:258) is named Namrud by the commentators, not the Quran.

name: Jurhum
story: When Hajar and the infant Ismail were alone in the valley of Makkah, the spring of Zamzam burst forth. A tribe from Yemen, Jurhum, saw birds circling and asked Hajar's permission to settle by the water. Ismail grew up among them, learned Arabic from them and married from them.
end: Tradition says Jurhum later grew corrupt as keepers of the Kaaba and were driven out by the tribe of Khuza'a; some say they buried Zamzam as they left.
lesson: Those who serve a sacred trust lose it when they betray it.
archaeology: Jurhum are known only from Arabic tradition; no inscription or excavation has identified them.
note: Their settling in Makkah is in Ibn Abbas's long hadith about Hajar and Ismail; the story of their expulsion comes from the historians.

name: People of Ilyas
story: Ilyas was sent to a people who worshipped an idol called Baal. He asked how they could call on Baal and abandon Allah, the best of creators, their Lord and the Lord of their fathers (37:125-126). They rejected him.
end: The Quran says they will be brought to account, except the sincere servants of Allah among them (37:127-128); it describes no worldly destruction.
lesson: False gods change their names, but the call to the One stays the same.
archaeology: Baal was a storm god widely worshipped in Canaan and Phoenicia, known from the texts of Ugarit (c. 1300 BCE). Some commentators linked Ilyas's people to Baalbek, whose huge Roman temples still stand.
note: The Bible places Elijah in the northern kingdom of Israel in the time of King Ahab; the Quran gives no place.

name: People of the Town (Ya-Sin)
story: Allah sent two messengers to a town, then strengthened them with a third (36:14). The people called them liars and threatened to stone them. A man came running from the far end of the city, urging his people to follow the messengers (36:20); the commentators say they killed him, and he was told to enter Paradise (36:26).
end: No army was sent down against them: there was only one shout, and they were extinguished (36:28-29).
lesson: One brave voice is remembered by Allah even when a whole city ignores it.
archaeology: Many commentators named the town Antioch (Antakya), where the mosque of Habib al-Najjar stands; it was badly damaged in the 2023 earthquake. Ibn Kathir doubted this, since Antioch was not destroyed and was an early Christian city.
note: The names of the messengers and of the man (Habib) come from the commentators, not the Quran.

name: The Sabians
story: The Quran names the Sabians three times beside the Jews and Christians (2:62, 5:69, 22:17). It promises that whoever of these believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good will have their reward. It gives no details of their beliefs.
end: Not ended: a people who carry the name survive today as the Mandaeans of Iraq and Iran.
lesson: Allah judges people by their faith and deeds, not by their labels.
archaeology: Who they were is debated: commentators suggested star-worshippers or followers of an old monotheism. Many modern scholars link them to the Mandaeans of the southern Iraqi marshes, who honour Yahya; the star-worshippers of Harran took the name under the Abbasids.

name: The Magians (Majus)
story: The Majus are the Zoroastrians of Persia, named once in the Quran among the religions Allah will judge between on the Day of Resurrection (22:17). Their faith taught a struggle between good and evil and honoured fire as pure. It was the state religion of the Persian empires the Muslims met.
end: Not ended: Zoroastrians still live in Iran and in India, where they are called Parsis. Under Muslim rule they paid the jizya and kept their worship.
lesson: The Quran names other faiths plainly and leaves the final judgement to Allah.
archaeology: Fire temples such as Takht-e Soleyman and the royal tombs of Naqsh-e Rostam survive in Iran. Their scripture, the Avesta, was written down under the Sasanians, and the date of their prophet Zarathustra is unknown.
note: A narration says to treat them like the People of the Book (Reported by Malik in the Muwatta); scholars discuss its chain.
